name: Kira Reyes

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Kira. I'm from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We're not tied to any company, union or party. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure. I'm a lead carpenter for a building co-op that does social housing, mostly timber-frame terraces out on the east side of the city. I'm on site by half six, I check the drawings against what got done yesterday, and I sort out my crew of five before the concrete people and the roofers start getting in each other's way. I'm also the union steward on site, so half my lunch break is somebody asking me about overtime or a bad ladder.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the moment a wall panel goes up and it's plumb first time, because that's my setting out and nobody else's. I love that a family is going to live in a house I built for rent they can actually afford. What wears me out is the paperwork and the apps the office keeps pushing at us. I still keep my notes in a pencil book, and my phone is for calls and nothing else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, that sounds like most things the office gets excited about. A big noise and then the same Monday morning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say what I always say on site: told you so. Every year there's some gadget that's going to change building, and every year we're still lifting joists by hand in the rain. I'd probably make a joke about it in the union group chat and leave it there.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, and I don't mind admitting it. I'm 27, I've put ten years into getting good at this, and I'd like those ten years to still count for something. If the only thing AI does is help the office do invoices, that's fine by me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different, really. I'd keep running my crew, keep putting money away like I do now, about a fifth of every pay packet. Maybe I'd finally take the joinery course I keep talking about, but that's for me, not because of any computer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Like a storm warning that turns out to be a bit of drizzle.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the office pushes apps at you. In this picture, would that pressure stop?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, they'd keep pushing, because somebody up there gets a bonus for it. There's a site diary app they want us all on, and I just hand my pencil book to Marta in the office every Friday and she types it up. If AI fizzles, that arrangement carries on and nobody gets hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your crew would be most glad to hear this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dario, my apprentice. He's 19 and he worries about this stuff more than any of us, he watches videos of robot bricklayers at lunch. I'd tell him, see, you picked a real trade, now stop watching that rubbish and learn to cut a birdsmouth properly.

S0.say: Told you so: every year there's a gadget that's meant to change building, and every year the crew is still lifting joists by hand in the rain. She'd joke about it in the union chat and move on.
S0.think: She'd be relieved, because ten years of getting good at carpentry would still count for something. If AI only helps the office with invoices, that suits her fine.
S0.do: Keeps running her crew and keeps saving about a fifth of each pay packet, as she does now. Might take a joinery course for her own interest, not because of AI.
S0.feel: Calm and a little smug, like a storm warning that turned into drizzle.
S0.quote: I just hand my pencil book to Marta in the office every Friday and she types it up.
S0.fieldNote: Kira's resistance to technology is personal and practical rather than angry: she has built a working life that keeps screens at arm's length. Her first thought goes to her apprentice, which says a lot about how she sees her role. Relief is the main note, with no sign of hidden worry in this picture.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Right. That one I can actually picture, because bits of it are already happening in the office.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is exactly why we need a strong union on every site. If tasks are getting taken over, workers should get a say in how, and a share of what the company saves. I'd bring it up at the next branch meeting, no question.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think my hands are safe for a good while, but the people around me might not be. The estimators, the site office, maybe the setting out with those laser machines. I'm the type who gets left behind when everyone else learns the new thing, and that bothers me more than I'd say out loud.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First I'd push the branch to get something written into our agreement about new tech, so nobody gets let go without retraining. I'd keep working the way I do, and I'd keep my savings where they are, about ten months' worth. If the co-op brought in some new system for my own job, I'd probably make someone show me three times and still grumble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit uneasy. Not scared, more like a stone in my boot I can't stop noticing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're the type who gets left behind. Can you give me an example of that happening before?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: When the co-op moved the timesheets onto a phone app two years ago, I was the last one on site still filling in paper. Marta covered for me for months. It wasn't a disaster, but I felt like a dinosaur in front of my own crew, and I'm supposed to be the lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you hold responsible if this went badly for people on your site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The developers and the tech firms who sell this stuff with a promise of cutting staff. Not the co-op, they're decent, but they'd be under pressure from the councils that fund them to come in cheaper. That's why the rules have to come from the top, not from each site fighting alone.

S1.say: This is exactly why every site needs a strong union, so workers get a say in how tasks are taken over and a share of the savings. She'd raise it at the next branch meeting.
S1.think: Her hands feel safe for a good while, but office staff and setting-out work might not be. She worries quietly that she's the one who gets left behind when everyone else learns the new system.
S1.do: Pushes her union branch to write new-technology rules and retraining into the site agreement. Keeps working as she does and keeps her ten months of savings untouched.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a stone in her boot she can't stop noticing.
S1.quote: I felt like a dinosaur in front of my own crew, and I'm supposed to be the lead.
S1.fieldNote: The public line is about collective rules, but the private worry is very personal: being the slow one in front of her own crew. She blames tech sellers and funders squeezing costs, not her employer. Her instinct is to organise rather than to learn the tools herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years? That's before Dario even finishes his apprenticeship. Okay. Go on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say out loud that this has to be stopped or slowed down by law, full stop. A company shouldn't be allowed to put robots on a housing site before there's a plan for the people they replace. I'd be on every picket and every petition going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be in real trouble. I'm good with timber and people, and I'm hopeless with screens, and in this picture the screens win. Two years isn't enough for someone like me to turn into someone else. I'd be the best carpenter nobody needs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop spending on anything big straight away. Noor and I were looking at a bigger flat, that would be off. I'd put more aside every month and get the union to demand a guaranteed wage for anyone replaced, and I'd write to every councillor I could find. In the first year after it arrives, I'd probably still turn up on site as long as there was a site to turn up to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. My stomach drops just thinking about it. I'd be lying awake next to Noor working out how long ten months of savings really lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Let's stay on that. How long do you think ten months of savings really lasts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: On paper, ten months. In real life, if Noor's hospital is fine, maybe two years if we're careful, because she earns decent money on nights. But if everything's going to robots, who says nursing is safe either? That's the bit that keeps me up, the both-of-us bit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Dario, your apprentice, the week this was announced?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know, and that's the worst part. I'd probably buy him lunch at the café by the gate and tell him to stick with the crew and stick with the union, because I wouldn't have anything smarter to say. Two years ago I told him a trade was the safest thing he could pick.

S2.say: This has to be stopped or slowed by law, and no company should put robots on a housing site before there's a plan for the people they replace. She'd join every picket and petition.
S2.think: She believes she'd be in real trouble, because she's strong with timber and people but weak with screens. Two years isn't enough time for her to become a different kind of worker.
S2.do: Cancels the plan for a bigger flat with Noor and saves harder each month. Pushes the union to demand a guaranteed wage for replaced workers and writes to councillors.
S2.feel: Alarmed and losing sleep, especially at the thought that Noor's job might not be safe either.
S2.quote: I'd be the best carpenter nobody needs.
S2.fieldNote: This is where her low comfort with technology meets a real threat, and the confidence she had in Steady Disruption is gone. Her strong savings help, but she counts them in months, not years. The detail that hurts most is that she once told her apprentice a trade was the safest choice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a little more breathing room, but not much. It's about how long it took me to get from apprentice to lead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Same as before, really: we need rules, and we need them before the robots arrive, not after. With five years, there's no excuse for the government to be caught out. I'd say that loudly to anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years would give me time to get properly angry and organised, which is something. I still don't see myself learning to programme a machine, but maybe I could find the bit of building the robots are worst at. Old houses, repairs, awkward jobs. That might buy me a few extra years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start saving harder from day one, maybe a third of my pay instead of a fifth, and I'd keep the bigger flat on hold. I'd get on the union's regional committee so I'm in the room when deals get made. Once it arrived, I'd try to shift toward repair work on older housing, because every street round here is full of crooked hundred-year-old houses no robot has seen yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but less sick than the two-year one. There's a plan, even if it's a plan I don't love.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said you'd never learn to programme a machine. With five years, would you really not try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fair question. I'd probably try once, if the union ran a course, and I'd hate it. I'm not saying I can't learn, I'm saying I'd rather spend five years fighting for decent rules than five years pretending I'm a computer person. Maybe that's stubborn. It probably is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you cut first to save that third of your pay?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Takeaways, for a start, we get food from the Turkish place on Fridays and that's real money over a year. And the holiday Noor and I do every summer by the lake would become every other summer. The van stays, though. The van is my office.

S3.say: We need rules before the robots arrive, and with five years' notice the government has no excuse to be caught out. She'd say so loudly to anyone.
S3.think: Five years gives her time to organise and maybe find work robots handle worst, like repairs on old, crooked houses. She still doesn't see herself learning to programme machines.
S3.do: Raises her savings from a fifth to a third of her pay and keeps the bigger flat on hold. Joins the union's regional committee and moves toward repair work on older housing once AGI arrives.
S3.feel: Anxious but steadier than with two years, because she has a plan, even one she doesn't love.
S3.quote: The van stays, though. The van is my office.
S3.fieldNote: The extra three years turn panic into a plan, but the plan is built around avoiding new technology rather than learning it. When challenged, she admits it's partly stubbornness. Her money choices are concrete and modest: takeaways and summer holidays go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37. Huh. That's a whole other life, isn't it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and if we waste it, that's on the politicians. There should be a proper national plan: retraining paid for, a wage floor, unions at the table. I'd be campaigning for that the whole decade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years almost makes it worse in a funny way, because there's no excuse for me not to change. With two years I could say it wasn't my fault. With ten, if I'm still standing there with my pencil book in 2036, that's on me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing my job, because there'd still be houses to build for years, and I'd keep saving about a third of my pay. I'd spend serious time in the union pushing for that national plan. Somewhere in the middle of the decade I'd probably train up as a site trainer or assessor, teaching apprentices, because that's the part of the job I'd fight hardest to keep human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, with a bit of guilt mixed in. Like knowing you should go to the dentist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said ten years leaves you no excuse. Is that pressure coming from you, or from people around you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly from me. Noor would never say it, she just quietly signed up for some AI course at the hospital. But I'd see her doing it and feel like the one still filling in paper timesheets again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If you did train as an assessor for apprentices, what would you want to teach them that a robot couldn't?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: How to read a site. Which labourer is having a bad day, which delivery driver is going to dump the timber in the wrong place, when the foreman is bluffing about the schedule. That's half of carpentry and it's not in any drawing.

S4.say: Ten years is a gift, and wasting it would be the politicians' fault. She'd campaign all decade for a national plan with paid retraining, a wage floor and unions at the table.
S4.think: Ten years almost feels worse because it removes her excuse not to change. If she's still holding her pencil book in 2036, she'd see that as her own fault.
S4.do: Keeps working and saving about a third of her pay while campaigning through the union for a national plan. Mid-decade, trains as a site trainer or assessor for apprentices.
S4.feel: Uneasy with some guilt, like knowing she should go to the dentist.
S4.quote: With two years I could say it wasn't my fault. With ten, if I'm still standing there with my pencil book in 2036, that's on me.
S4.fieldNote: An interesting twist: more time brings less fear but more personal responsibility, and she feels it as guilt. Her chosen escape is teaching, which keeps her close to the human side of the trade she values. Her partner quietly learning AI is a pressure she doesn't voice at home.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, easily. That's the one where being stubborn costs me everything and there's no time to fix it. What would help is a guaranteed income for anyone pushed out, decided by law before the machines show up, and retraining that's run by people from the trade, not some app.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who builds the robots' houses. I'm half joking. But really, somebody has to decide whether we use this to build more homes for people who need them, or just to cut wages. That's the question I'd want people to argue about.

headlineQuote: Two years ago I told him a trade was the safest thing he could pick.
portrait: Kira Reyes is a 27-year-old lead carpenter and union steward on a co-op social housing site, proud of her setting out and stubbornly attached to her pencil notebook. She is calm about the AI Plateau and only uneasy about Steady Disruption, trusting the union to set rules. The two-year AGI picture alarms her, because it hits her weak spot with technology before she can adapt, and she worries about her partner's nursing job too. With five or ten years she builds a plan around repairs, teaching apprentices and campaigning, though she admits the extra time also leaves her without an excuse.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because being slow with technology would cost her everything and there would be no time to fix it.
whatWouldHelp: A guaranteed income for anyone pushed out, set in law before the machines arrive, and retraining run by people from the trade rather than through an app.
